Zambia Recalls 2018 Cyber Attack on National Payments System

Zambia’s business community is reflecting on the lasting lessons of the 2018 cyber attack that disrupted the nation’s electronic payments infrastructure, causing widespread economic disruption. While no current disruptions persist, the incident remains a cautionary tale for the rapidly digitizing Zambian economy.

On March 6, 2018, the Bank of Zambia’s National Payments Platform, run by the Lusaka-based fintech provider Zampay Solutions, was targeted by an unknown group of hackers. The attack forced the suspension of electronic fund transfers and card payments at ATMs and point-of-sale terminals for nearly 48 hours. Mobile money services, which underpin much of Zambia’s retail economy, were also affected.

The Zambia Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimated that daily retail sales declined by more than 30 percent during the outage. “It was a wake-up call,” said Chamber President Grace Mwale. “Businesses across the country, from Lusaka to Kitwe, faced significant losses, and informal traders suffered as cash reserves dried up.”

Telecommunications and power services remained unaffected, but the payment system disruption rippled through supply chains, delaying fuel deliveries at ports and stalling payrolls for several large employers.

A government inquiry attributed the breach to a combination of outdated software and weak network segmentation. “We have since invested over $12 million in cybersecurity upgrades,” said National Payments Director John Chilemba, while confirming that no customer funds were lost. “Our new protocols include regular system audits and mandatory employee training.”

Analysts note that the 2018 incident accelerated reforms. “Zambia’s payments sector is significantly more resilient today,” said independent fintech consultant Tinashe Banda. “But as digital adoption grows, vigilance is essential.”

The 2018 attack remains one of the most significant cyber threats to hit Zambia’s economic infrastructure, shaping policy and investment to this day.
